title: bell hooks
tradition: Feminism and the ethic of love
keyWorks: Teaching to Transgress: Education as the Practice of Freedom (1994)
Communion: The Female Search for Love (2002)
The Will to Change: Men, Masculinity, and Love (2004)
summary: bell hooks (1952–2021; born Gloria Jean Watkins) was an American writer, feminist thinker and teacher from Kentucky. She took her pen name from her great-grandmother and wrote it in lowercase so that attention would go to her ideas rather than to her person. She wrote about love, education, race, class and gender as things that touch everyone's everyday life — in clear language addressed not only to scholars.
onEmotions: For hooks, feelings are never a purely private matter: the way we feel shame, fear or love is largely learned in the family and in the culture. She called a society built on hierarchy and control a “dominator culture” and showed that it rests on fear and shame and teaches us to hide vulnerability. hooks's answer is a “love ethic.” Love, for her, is not a feeling that simply happens but an action and a choice: following M. Scott Peck, she defines it as the will to nurture growth — your own and another person's — and following Erich Fromm she names its ingredients: care, responsibility, respect and knowledge, to which she adds trust, commitment and honest communication. She considered self-love and self-esteem the starting point, and healing a shared rather than a solitary task. Where there is abuse and humiliation there is no love — but the capacity to love can be learned anew.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is not weakness or whim: it is how the psyche responds to a world in which much really is unreliable. bell hooks wrote about “dominator culture” — her name for a society built on hierarchy, competition and control — and noticed that in it people constantly feel judged and threatened. If anxiety has become the background of your life, it is not only your personal problem. From hooks's point of view, you could say that the opposite of anxiety is not fearlessness but connection: trust, honest conversation, care. Anxiety eases not when we “pull ourselves together” alone, but when we stop hiding it from those we can trust. Perhaps right now your anxiety is asking not for strictness but for care — including your own.
anxiety.practice: Write one sentence about your anxiety the way you would tell it to someone you trust. Think about which living person you might one day say it to.

fear.text: Fear is an ancient and honest feeling: it wants to keep you safe. In All About Love bell hooks observed that fear is the main force holding up relations of domination: it pushes us to separate, to hide, to avoid being known. That's why she set against fear not heroism but love, understood as action. This doesn't mean being afraid is shameful. It means fear has a counterweight available even on a very small scale: one step toward someone, one honest sentence, one request for help. From hooks's point of view, you could say that fear narrows the world down to “me against everyone,” and love widens it again. You don't need to stop being afraid first in order to make a tiny move toward connection with another person.
fear.practice: Think of one person around whom you feel a little less afraid. Write down what exactly about them gives you that feeling — and, if you like, let them know they matter to you.

quote.text: When we choose to love we choose to move against fear—against alienation and separation. The choice to love is a choice to connect—to find ourselves in the other.
quote.author: bell hooks

sadness.text: Sadness deserves room and time. bell hooks wrote a great deal about how our culture teaches us to hide sadness — boys and men especially, but really all of us — as if it were a sign of weakness or ingratitude. In The Will to Change she showed how costly the emotional numbness that passes for strength can be. From her point of view, allowing yourself to be sad is part of loving yourself: care begins with attention to what you actually feel, not to what you are “supposed” to feel. hooks spoke of love as a practice, and one of its simplest forms is to acknowledge, “I'm sad right now,” without demanding that you fix yourself immediately. Sadness that is seen and accepted stays heavy, but it stops being lonely.
sadness.practice: Place your hand where you feel the sadness in your body and silently tell yourself: “I see that you're sad.” Stay like this for a minute without changing anything.

grief.text: Grief is love that has nowhere left to go, and it has the right to last as long as it lasts. In All About Love bell hooks devoted a whole chapter to loss. She noticed that our culture hurries the bereaved — “time to move on” — and so leaves them alone with what remains unsaid. For hooks, love doesn't end with death: care, memory and gratitude continue as action — in how we speak of the one who is gone, in what we keep, in what we learned from them. She also insisted that it is better to grieve not in isolation but in community, among those who can share your tears and your stories. Grief doesn't need to be “done right” or quickly; it needs to be lived through — ideally with support.
grief.practice: Write down one thing that the person you lost taught you. If you feel like it, tell someone that story today.

loneliness.text: Loneliness truly hurts, and behind it lies a real need — to be known and needed. bell hooks believed many people in modern culture live in a state of “lovelessness” — not because something is wrong with them, but because the culture values success, consumption and independence more than connection. At the same time hooks distinguished loneliness as being abandoned from solitude as a choice. She considered the ability to be with yourself part of the art of loving: someone who can be alone with themselves comes to others not to escape but to meet them. Her answer to loneliness is not to urgently find “the one,” but to gradually grow circles of community: friends, neighbors, people with whom you can share care. Love, she wrote, doesn't live only in couples.
loneliness.practice: Think of someone with whom the connection has weakened but was once warm. Send them a short message — for no reason and with no expectations.

anger.text: Anger can be precise: it notices injustice before reason finds the words. bell hooks was not afraid of anger. In Killing Rage, her collection of essays on racism, she wrote about her own rage at the injustice she had lived through and insisted that anger can be a healthy response to oppression rather than a flaw of character. But she also distinguished anger that helps us see and act from anger that turns into a wish to dominate another. Her “love ethic” — a life in which care, respect and justice become the main guides — doesn't ask you to suppress anger. It asks what the anger is serving: the defense of dignity or the destruction of connection. Anger that is listened to carefully often points to a value that has been hurt.
anger.practice: Finish the sentence: “I'm angry because what matters to me is…” The answer will show what your anger is protecting.

shame.text: Shame is one of the heaviest feelings, because it says not “I did something bad” but “I am bad.” bell hooks wrote that shaming is a familiar tool of power: in families, schools and society people are often raised through humiliation, and the mark lasts a long time. In All About Love she recalled that in her childhood harshness and punishment were called love — and only with time did she understand that care and shaming are incompatible. For hooks, shame grows in silence and isolation and weakens when it can be spoken aloud in the presence of someone who won't judge. This doesn't mean you have to open up to everyone. But it does mean your shame is not a verdict — often it is an imprint of how you were once treated.
shame.practice: Ask yourself: whose voice is my shame speaking in right now? Write down whether that person (or that environment) could have been wrong about you.

guilt.text: Guilt shows that you care how your actions affect others. Drawing on Erich Fromm, bell hooks included responsibility in the very definition of love: to love means to answer for how we affect those around us. But responsibility, for her, is not endless self-punishment. Self-flagellation, as her thinking suggests, locks us up in ourselves and gets in the way of doing what really matters: acknowledging what we did, apologizing, making amends where possible. hooks valued honesty above flawlessness: anyone can make a mistake, and love is tested by what we do after it. Guilt can be turned from a burden into a step — not “what a terrible person I am,” but “what can I do now.”
guilt.practice: Name one concrete small action that could acknowledge or repair what you feel guilty about. You don't have to do it today — naming it is enough.

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant but very human, and behind it there is often a wish worth hearing. In the chapter on greed in All About Love, bell hooks wrote that consumer culture trains us to measure our worth by what we have and how we look next to others. In that logic, someone else's good fortune feels like a personal loss. hooks offered a different measure — the values we live by: care, generosity, community. From her point of view, you could say that envy shows not that you are a bad person but what you are missing — recognition, rest, opportunities, love. If you translate envy into a question about your own needs, it stops being poison and becomes a clue.
envy.practice: Name what exactly about the other person makes you envious, and then which need of yours this reflects. Write down only the second.

emptiness.text: Emptiness is a strange feeling: as if there were nothing inside to hold on to. bell hooks wrote about “lovelessness” as a quiet epidemic: many people grew up without the experience of reliable, attentive care and later try to fill that lack with things, work, entertainment, other people's approval. This is not your fault — it happens when a culture offers consumption instead of connection. For hooks, the way out begins not with a great feeling but with small practices of love: attention to yourself, honesty, regular care for your body and for those around you. Love, for her, is a verb, not a state; you can start doing it even when it's quiet and empty inside. Sometimes the feeling follows the action rather than preceding it.
emptiness.practice: Do one small thing for yourself as you would for someone you love: pour a warm drink, open a window, wrap yourself in a blanket. Notice how it feels.

confusion.text: Confusion often comes when old words and explanations stop working. The first chapter of All About Love is called “Clarity”: bell hooks begins by saying that many people are confused about love because no one ever really defined it for them. Her lesson is that clarity is born through words: naming, distinguishing, defining. In Teaching to Transgress she described education as “the practice of freedom” — a space where you can not know, ask questions and think together without fear of looking foolish. From her point of view, confusion is not failure but the beginning of thinking. A question asked honestly is already moving you toward understanding, even if the answer doesn't come right away.
confusion.practice: Pick one word that is surrounded by the most confusion for you right now (for example, “work,” “home,” “relationship”) and write your own definition of it — even a rough one.

fatigue.text: Fatigue is not laziness or a flaw of character; it is a body and soul that have long carried more than they could manage. In Sisters of the Yam bell hooks wrote about “self-recovery” — about how people, especially women used to caring for everyone but themselves, are worn out by endless giving. For hooks, self-care is not selfishness but part of the love ethic: you can't love others sustainably if you treat yourself as a free resource. She also noticed that a culture that prizes productivity makes rest seem suspicious. From her point of view, you could say that your fatigue is a legitimate request for care, and listening to it is also a way of loving.
fatigue.practice: Name one obligation that could be postponed, simplified or handed over today. Give yourself permission out loud.

boredom.text: Boredom can mean there is little around you that truly touches you. In Teaching to Transgress bell hooks wrote that learning should be exciting, and that boredom in the classroom is not the student's fault but a sign that knowledge has been cut off from life, body and feelings. Her “engaged pedagogy” called for the participation of the whole person, not just the head. From hooks's point of view, you could say that boredom in life is like a boring lesson: we play our roles without asking what actually interests us. Boredom is worth listening to rather than drowning out — it may be calling you toward curiosity, a lively conversation, something that touches you personally.
boredom.practice: Write down a question you would genuinely like to know the answer to — any question, even a strange one. Spend five minutes beginning to explore it.

joy.text: Joy is a celebration, and it needs no justification. bell hooks wrote that love is not only work and responsibility but also pleasure: real closeness brings joy, lightness, laughter. She valued joy shared with others — at shared meals, in conversations, in a classroom where learning suddenly became exciting. For people who have lived through hardship, joy for hooks is also an affirmation of their own humanity: the capacity to delight in life even when the world is pressing down. From her point of view, joy doesn't cancel seriousness or make you frivolous; it feeds the strength for love and care. Let yourself notice it fully, in all its details.
joy.practice: Tell someone about your joy — or at least write down whom you would like to share it with.

love.text: Love is bell hooks's central theme. In All About Love she suggests not describing love as a feeling that simply “happens,” but understanding it as action and choice. Following the psychiatrist M. Scott Peck, she defines love as the will to extend oneself for the sake of spiritual growth — one's own or another person's. And following Erich Fromm, she names its ingredients: care, responsibility, respect, knowledge — and adds trust, commitment and honest communication. Such a definition is freeing: to love means not only to feel something strongly but to do what helps you both grow. Your feeling is valuable in itself, and hooks invites you to give it shape in actions.
love.practice: Choose one ingredient of love — care, respect, knowledge or trust — and today do one thing in its spirit toward someone close to you or toward yourself.

quote.text: The will to extend one's self for the purpose of nurturing one's own or another's spiritual growth.
quote.author: M. Scott Peck
quote.source: The Road Less Traveled (1978); bell hooks makes this definition the foundation of All About Love

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling that reminds us: we don't create ourselves alone. bell hooks often remembered with gratitude those who supported her — including the Black women teachers of the segregated school of her childhood. In Teaching to Transgress she wrote that these women taught with devotion, seeing the future in their students, and that learning was then a joy for her. For hooks, gratitude is tied to recognition — one of the ingredients of love: to see what another has done for you and to say it out loud. From her point of view, you could say that gratitude is love turned back through time: it connects us to a chain of care that stretches across generations.
gratitude.practice: Write a short thank-you to someone who once believed in you — even if you never send it.

hope.text: Hope is the courage to expect good even when the grounds are fragile. One of bell hooks's books is titled simply Teaching Community: A Pedagogy of Hope. For her, hope is not passive waiting but a practice: we hope when we keep building connections, learning and caring without seeing any guarantee of the outcome. hooks was inspired by the Brazilian educator Paulo Freire, for whom hope was inseparable from action. From her point of view, hope is especially needed where it seems nothing is changing — and it holds up better together with others. Your hope is not naive: it is part of the effort by which people in every age have made life better.
hope.practice: Name one small action this week that nourishes your hope, and one person you could share it with.

quote.text: The moment we choose to love we begin to move against domination, against oppression. The moment we choose to love we begin to move towards freedom.
quote.author: bell hooks
quote.source: Outlaw Culture (1994), “Love as the Practice of Freedom”

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a longing for the place and time that shaped us, and it has its own tenderness. Toward the end of her life bell hooks returned to her native Kentucky and wrote Belonging: A Culture of Place — about the hills, the land and the people of her childhood. She didn't idealize the past: there was much pain and injustice in it. But she knew how to recognize what had nourished her — for example, what she called “homeplace”: the home where Black families created a space of dignity and care in a world that denied it to them. From her point of view, nostalgia needs neither to be rejected nor turned into a cult. You can ask: what exactly from the past do I want to bring with me into the present?
nostalgia.practice: Recall one detail from the past that you miss, and think about how its spirit (not its form) could be let into today.

craving.text: A craving is a strong wave, and being swept up by it doesn't mean you are weak. In All About Love bell hooks wrote that a culture short on love pushes people to seek comfort in consumption: things, food and endless entertainment promise to fill the lack quickly — and without the risk of being rejected. From her point of view, you could say that a craving often points not only to its object but also to what that object is standing in for: rest, closeness, relief, the feeling that you matter to someone. This understanding is not an order to “stop wanting.” It simply places a second question next to the first: what am I actually missing right now? The wave rises and falls; you can wait it out with kindness toward yourself.
craving.practice: When a craving rises, ask yourself: “If this were about a feeling rather than a thing, what feeling would it be?” Write the answer in one word.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure, and shame is a poor helper here. bell hooks linked the prevalence of addiction to a culture in which people lack reliable care and in which consumption promises to replace closeness. If love for hooks is always a choice, a will to grow, then addiction gradually takes away precisely a person's freedom to choose; so it is not a matter of strength of character but of an unfreedom anyone can fall into. The way out, from her point of view, is not a lonely battle but the restoring of connections: healing, she wrote, almost never happens in isolation. In many mutual-help communities people do exactly this — meet themselves and one another without judgment. You deserve care right now, not only “later.”
addiction.practice: Think about whether there is at least one person or group nearby with whom you could talk about your struggle without shame. You don't need to decide anything — just note that such a path exists.

hangover.text: The morning after — your body is heavy, your head holds only fragments, and shame is often standing close by. bell hooks wrote that shame is a poor teacher: it drives a person into silence and isolation, and isolation usually only makes things heavier. Her alternative is responsibility without self-abasement, as in Fromm: acknowledging what happened and taking care of the consequences and of yourself. From the point of view of her love ethic, you could say that what you need now is not verdicts but care: water, rest, quiet, a warm word. You can work out what happened and why later, when you feel better. Treating yourself kindly on a hard morning doesn't mean approving of everything that happened; it means not abandoning yourself.
hangover.practice: Do one caring thing for your body right now — drink some water, wash your face, open the window a little — and mentally set aside going over yesterday until later.

euphoria.text: A high, when the world is shining and everything seems possible, is a wonderful feeling, and you can simply live it. bell hooks treasured such moments: she wrote about the excitement that sweeps through a classroom when an idea suddenly comes alive, and about the joy of conversation and community as an almost bodily experience. From her point of view, you could say that a high is fullest when it is shared: joy experienced together becomes a bridge to others. hooks also valued clarity — not to cool the delight, but so that it doesn't carry you away from the people close to you and from yourself. Enjoy this state and stay connected: tell someone you're feeling good right now.
euphoria.practice: Write down in a word or two what is making you so happy right now, so you can remember it later. And share it with one person.

crash.text: The drop after a high can be sharp: yesterday it seemed you could handle anything, and today it's hard even to get up. This is a very human experience, and it doesn't cancel the value of the good that was. bell hooks named commitment as one of the ingredients of love: being there not only on the joyful days. From her point of view, you could say that you can make the same commitment to yourself — not to abandon yourself when your strength has gone. Instead of demanding the old high from yourself, her love ethic would suggest gentle attention: what do you need right now to get through this day? The swings of feeling don't define you; what remains is your ability to care for yourself at both the high point and the low.
crash.practice: Make a list of three very small tasks for today, including one just for pleasure. Tick off each one, however small.

panic.text: Panic is terrifying: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it seems it will always be like this. It really is hard, and you are not exaggerating. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. bell hooks considered the Buddhist teacher Thich Nhat Hanh one of her mentors and valued the practice of mindfulness — returning to the present through the body and the breath. She insisted that a person is a unity of mind, body and spirit, not just thoughts. From her point of view, you could say that in a moment of panic there is nothing you need to understand or solve. You only need to come back to your body and wait out the wave — the way you would hold the hand of a frightened friend.
panic.practice: Place both feet on the floor and feel the support. Take a few breaths with the exhale longer than the inhale, and name out loud five objects you see around you.

dread.text: A heavy premonition that something bad is about to happen is exhausting. You don't have to be ashamed of it or force it away. bell hooks wrote that fear makes us hide and separate from others — and it is in isolation that it grows. She didn't promise that the world is safe: she knew well how much cruelty is in it. But she found support in connection — in people with whom you can share the load, and in practices of mindfulness that bring you back to the present. From her point of view, you could say that a premonition speaks of the future, but we can only live now — and right now you are here, you are breathing. For today, it is enough to live through today.
dread.practice: Write down what exactly you will do in the next hour. Only the next hour — the rest can wait.

fomo.text: The feeling that life is happening somewhere else, to other people, is especially strong when we constantly see others' hand-picked moments. bell hooks wrote that consumer culture turns happiness into a shop window and makes us compare our lives with images created to sell. From her point of view, you could say that the fear of missing out is largely a product of that shop window, not accurate knowledge of what you lack. Her love ethic suggests looking not wider but deeper: what in your own life is already waiting for attention and care — a friendship, an activity, a place? Fullness, for hooks, comes not from the quantity of experiences but from presence and connection.
fomo.practice: Put your phone away for ten minutes and write down three things in your life that you wouldn't want to miss — not other people's, your own.

sleepless.text: A sleepless night can be very lonely: the world is asleep, and your thoughts keep circling. You are not alone in this, and you are not doing anything “wrong.” Drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh's tradition of mindfulness, bell hooks spoke of the wholeness of body, mind and spirit — and of how caring for yourself means listening to your body rather than giving it orders. From her point of view, you could say that at night the mind tends to exaggerate what is hard, so right now you don't need to solve a single question. You can simply treat yourself like a loved one who can't fall asleep: gently, without reproach, without hurry. Rest is not only sleep; lying quietly in the dark also restores you little by little.
sleepless.practice: Place your palm on your chest, take a few slow exhales and silently tell yourself: “Nothing needs to be decided right now.”

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds especially deeply because it strikes at trust itself — the foundation the relationship stood on. Your pain is understandable. In All About Love bell hooks calls trust and honesty essential ingredients of love, and lying one of the main reasons love is so fragile in our culture. She noticed that many people are taught from childhood to lie for convenience and to “keep the peace in the family,” and this habit later destroys intimacy. From her point of view, betrayal is not proof of your naivety but a violation for which the one who committed it is responsible. Your capacity to trust is not a weakness but something of value, worth protecting.
betrayal.practice: Write down what the betrayal told you about the other person — and separately, what it does NOT say about your worth.

jealousy.text: Jealousy grips the heart with the fear of losing someone dear. Almost everyone knows this feeling. In All About Love bell hooks wrote that our culture teaches us to confuse love with possession: as if loving meant owning and controlling a person. For hooks, love rests on respect and mutuality — on recognizing the other's freedom. From her point of view, you could say that jealousy often speaks less about the other person than about our own insecurity — the fear that we are not enough, and a lack of trust. This is not a verdict but an invitation: to notice your vulnerability and take care of it, instead of demanding guarantees from the other.
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence: “What I'm most afraid of is that…”. Then ask yourself what would help you feel more secure — without control.

resentment.text: A grudge that won't let go for years is heavy — and it almost always has a reason: you really were hurt. In All About Love bell hooks wrote about forgiveness as a gift we give first of all to ourselves, to free ourselves from the power of the past. But forgiveness, for her, doesn't mean forgetting or excusing: you can acknowledge that you were treated unjustly and still consider it unjust. Forgiveness is a process, not a duty, and it can't be forced. From her point of view, you could say that resentment keeps the memory of the wound, and first it needs to be heard. Only pain that has been acknowledged can, over time, loosen its grip.
resentment.practice: Write a letter you won't send: what you would like this person to understand about your pain.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts with your whole body, and there is nothing shameful in that. bell hooks wrote that many of us learned about love in places where it was mixed with pain, and so a breakup often touches not only the present loss but old wounds too. At the same time her view offers support: if love is action and choice, then the capacity to love doesn't leave along with the person. It stays in you — in your care, your openness, your ability to trust — and you can direct it toward yourself and others. hooks insisted that we heal together: friends, loved ones, community can hold you while your heart mends. The strength of the pain is a sign of how deeply you are able to attach.
heartbreak.practice: Call or message someone who knows how to listen and say honestly: “I'm having a hard time right now.” You don't have to explain anything more.

quote.text: Rarely, if ever, are any of us healed in isolation. Healing is an act of communion.
quote.author: bell hooks

impostor.text: The feeling that you're here by accident and about to be “found out” is very common — especially among those who have come to a new environment from far away. bell hooks grew up in a working-class family in the American South, and in Teaching to Transgress and Where We Stand: Class Matters she wrote about how out of place she felt at an elite university, where different manners, language and confidence were valued. She came to understand that this feeling was not proof of her inadequacy but a consequence of the rules of the game having been set by others. From her point of view, you could say that your “impostor” feeling often speaks of the distance you have traveled, not of a shortcoming. And the experience of a person “from the margins” is valuable: hooks called the margin a space of “radical openness.”
impostor.practice: Write down three things you know how to do or understand precisely because of your path — because of where you came from.

self_hatred.text: When an inner voice keeps saying that you are bad, unwanted, unworthy, it hurts a great deal. That voice is not telling the truth about you. bell hooks wrote that many people absorb in childhood the shaming and neglect they experienced from adults and later repeat them to themselves; this is not your nature but something learned. In All About Love and Rock My Soul she called self-love the foundation of all love and wrote about practices of self-esteem, among them self-acceptance: the decision to be on your own side even before the feeling has arrived. For hooks, love is action: you can treat yourself gently even without believing you deserve it. You do deserve it.
self_hatred.practice: Ask yourself: what would I say to a friend who spoke about themselves in these words? Write it to yourself — even just one sentence.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a heavy feeling: it seems nothing depends on you. Sometimes that is partly true: there are circumstances one person can't change. bell hooks knew well the power of large systems — racism, poverty, patriarchy — and never blamed people for being unable to defeat them alone. But she wrote about the move “from object to subject”: from being someone things are done to, to being someone who speaks and acts, however modestly. Her image of “homeplace” speaks to the same thing: people deprived of power in society created spaces of dignity and care at home. From her point of view, when the big things are beyond your power, the small ones are still yours.
helplessness.practice: Draw two circles: in one, what doesn't depend on you right now; in the other, one small thing that does. Focus on the second.

procrastination.text: Putting things off is not laziness. More often fear is hiding behind it: of not coping, of being judged, of seeing the gap between the idea and the result. bell hooks, the author of more than thirty books, spoke in Remembered Rapture: The Writer at Work about writing as a practice you learn, not a gift for the chosen few. In Teaching to Transgress she criticized an education in which mistakes are shamed and in which learning therefore becomes frightening. From her point of view, you could say that if fear of judgment lies behind your procrastination, what helps is not pressure but a kinder environment — including an inner one. Give yourself the right to an imperfect first step: a draft is not a verdict, but a beginning.
procrastination.practice: Do the tiniest, most “wrong” version of the first step — for example, write one bad sentence. Five minutes is enough.

uprooted.text: The sense of being cut off from your roots is vivid and heavy. You can live in a new place for years and still not feel at home. bell hooks spent many years in big cities far from Kentucky, and in Belonging: A Culture of Place she described how she longed for the land, the hills and the people of her childhood, and how she eventually returned. But the main thing she shows is that belonging is not only a point on a map; it is a practice of connection with land, people and memory. From her point of view, you could say that roots can not only be lost but also grown — by strengthening the threads to the past and making new ones where you are now. Your longing shows how much belonging matters to you.
uprooted.practice: Choose one habit or thing from “home” — a dish, a song, a word — and let it into your current life this week.

overload.text: When there's too much of everything — tasks, news, other people's expectations — it's hard even to think. This is not a personal failure: many people today live at a pace that leaves no room for a breather. bell hooks wrote that a culture of domination and consumption encourages endless busyness and places almost no value on silence, contemplation, rest. Spiritual life — for her not necessarily religion, but a practice of inner quiet and attention — was a source of clarity and of the strength to love. From her point of view, you could say that overload takes away our ability to be attentive to ourselves and to others, and so our ability to love. Protecting your time and your quiet is care, not selfishness.
overload.practice: Choose one thing you can skip today or do less well than usual. Spend the minutes you free up in silence.

unreality.text: The feeling that the world or you yourself have become unreal, as if behind glass, is frightening and disorienting. Many people know this experience, and it can be talked about calmly. bell hooks didn't write about it directly, but in Teaching to Transgress she criticized the habit of separating mind and body — as if thinking happened somewhere apart from the living, feeling person. She insisted on wholeness: we are body, mind and spirit all at once. From her point of view, you could say that when reality seems to recede, what gently helps is returning to bodily presence and to other people — to what is warm, tangible, simple. This feeling comes in waves, and it doesn't make you any less real.
unreality.practice: Pick up an object with a distinct texture and describe out loud its weight, temperature and surface. Then say out loud the name of the place where you are.

awe.text: Awe is a rare feeling, when the world suddenly turns out to be bigger than we thought and everything inside goes quiet. bell hooks considered spirituality an important part of the love ethic and wrote that she grew up among the hills of Kentucky, where nature taught her a sense of connection with all living things. In Belonging the land appears as something that restores both humility and joy. From her point of view, you could say that awe is the moment when hierarchies and competition recede and we feel part of a larger whole. You don't need to do anything with it — only let it be and perhaps remember how it feels in your body.
awe.practice: Stay for a minute with whatever filled you with awe. Then write down one word you'd like to carry away with you.

relief.text: Relief is like finally being able to breathe out. This feeling deserves attention: it shows how much tension you were carrying. bell hooks wrote that many people become so used to constant pressure that they take it for normal. From her point of view, you could say that it is the moment of relief that reveals how hard things were — and it is a good time for self-care: to acknowledge that you've been through something difficult and let your body rest. Relief can also hint at what exactly was so heavy, so that you can notice it sooner in the future. Just let yourself enjoy the lightness — without rushing to the next task.
relief.practice: Take a long exhale and write down: what exactly has ended or let go? Mark it as a small celebration.

calm.text: Calm is a precious state, and it's good simply to feel it fully. Inspired by the Buddhist teacher Thich Nhat Hanh, bell hooks valued mindfulness — the ability to be fully in the present. She called spiritual practices — meditation, prayer, silence — a source from which to draw strength for love and for work in the world. From her point of view, you could say that calm is not detachment but a foundation: from it, it's easier to listen, understand and respond to others with care rather than with a jolt. In a culture that prizes haste such minutes are easy to dismiss as useless, but for hooks they are part of caring for yourself, not its opposite. Stay in it; nothing needs to be added.
calm.practice: Notice three sensations in your body that are telling you about calm right now. Remember them — you can come back to them.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the excitement of an idea coming alive and making you want to act. bell hooks knew it well: she wrote about the “excitement” in a classroom when teacher and students discover something new together, and considered this feeling a legitimate part of thinking rather than an obstacle to it. For her, learning and creating meant taking part as a whole person — with your body, your feelings, your life experience. From her point of view, you could say that inspiration grows in dialogue: you want to share it, and sharing makes it stronger. Let it be, write your ideas down while they're hot, and don't rush to judge them: criticism can wait, and living excitement is easily scared off.
inspiration.practice: Write the idea down in raw form, without editing. Think about whom you could discuss it with in the next few days.

quote.text: The classroom remains the most radical space of possibility in the academy.
quote.author: bell hooks
quote.source: Teaching to Transgress: Education as the Practice of Freedom (1994)

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — secret pleasure at someone else's failure — brings shame, but almost everyone knows this feeling. Having it doesn't make you a bad person. bell hooks wrote that “dominator culture” trains us to think in hierarchies: who is above, who is below, who won, who lost. In that picture, someone else's fall feels like your own rise. From her point of view, you could say that schadenfreude often speaks of an old hurt, or of times when you yourself felt humiliated and unrecognized. The love ethic doesn't shame you for this feeling; it invites you to ask: which wound of mine just responded? When a wound is noticed, the wish for someone else to suffer usually loses its force.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: what do I myself want of what this other person has just lost? Write down the answer — that is your need.

contempt.text: Contempt is a cold feeling: it places the other beneath you. Sometimes it arises as a defense — when we have been hurt, or when someone has behaved truly badly. bell hooks saw clearly how society teaches contempt — for the poor, for women, for those who are “different” — and how contempt props up hierarchies. Her love ethic is built on respect, one of the ingredients of love in Erich Fromm: seeing the other as they are, not through a label. This doesn't mean approving of what others do. From her point of view, you could say that contempt often protects us from pain or from the fear of turning out to be like the person we despise. It's worth asking what exactly it is covering up.
contempt.practice: Finish the sentence: “If I didn't despise this person, I would have to feel…”. See what word appears.

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong bodily reaction: you want to turn away, to pull back. It can be directed at a situation, at people, sometimes at yourself. bell hooks showed that culture often teaches disgust toward certain bodies and groups of people, and that such disgust — learned, not natural — sustains injustice. But there is also disgust that honestly reports, “this is unacceptable to me” — and it deserves respect as a boundary. From her point of view, you could say that it matters to tell where your disgust comes from — from your own values or from other people's judgments you have absorbed. If it is aimed at yourself, it's worth asking whose words you are hearing. Perhaps you were simply taught to look at yourself that way.
disgust.practice: Ask yourself: is this disgust protecting something I value, or repeating someone else's judgment? Write down what you noticed.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge usually arises where there was real pain or injustice. It is an understandable feeling, and behind it is a need for your wound to be acknowledged. bell hooks didn't deny anger at injustice, but she clearly distinguished the pursuit of justice from the urge to cause pain in return. Her love ethic starts from the view that violence and domination, even in retaliation, continue the very cycle we want to leave. From her point of view, you could say that revenge promises to restore dignity, but dignity is restored more through acknowledgment, support and the protection of your boundaries. The feeling can be lived through fully — in words, on paper, in conversation with someone who understands — without turning it into an act against anyone.
revenge.practice: Write down what exactly the person who hurt you would have to understand or acknowledge. This will show what your real need is.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those closest to you — a partner, parents, children — is a very common feeling, and so is shame about it. Being angry with the people you love doesn't mean loving them less. bell hooks wrote that love is not a constant warm feeling but a practice of care, respect and responsibility in which there is room for difficult emotions too. She also stressed that where there is love there is no place for abuse and humiliation — and this applies to how we express anger. From her point of view, you could say that anger at someone close often points to an unmet need — for rest, respect, help — and to the fact that it hasn't yet been spoken about. The task is not to stop being angry but to find words and a safe form for the anger.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger rises, pause for a few breaths, then begin your sentence with “I need…” instead of “You always…”. You can practice on paper first.

ambivalence.text: Loving and being unable to stand the same person at once is not hypocrisy but a truth of close relationships that almost everyone knows. bell hooks wrote openly about her family — about people she loved and who also caused her pain. She showed that care and hurt can be joined in a relationship, and that acknowledging both doesn't destroy love but makes it more honest. For hooks, love is a choice and an action, not a demand to feel only warm feelings. From her point of view, you could say that you don't have to choose one feeling and cancel the other. You can hold them together and ask yourself which actions match your values.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a sheet into two columns: “what I value in this person” and “what I find hard to bear.” Fill in both without drawing a conclusion.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, leaving a job or even the death of a seriously ill loved one is often accompanied by shame: “how can I be glad about this?” You can. Relief and love don't contradict each other. bell hooks wrote that love includes care and responsibility, and these can be very heavy, especially when they go on for a long time. Relief often shows how much strength you were giving. For hooks, loss is part of love, and grief weaves together all kinds of feelings. From her point of view, you could say that relief doesn't cancel your attachment; it honestly marks the end of strain. Allow yourself to feel both, without choosing the “right” one.
guilty_relief.practice: Write one sentence: “I feel relieved, and at the same time I…” — and finish it with whatever is also true.

indifference.text: Sometimes, where something “should” move you, everything inside is quiet — and that feels unsettling. In The Will to Change bell hooks wrote about how many people, especially boys, are taught from childhood to switch off their feelings in order to survive in an environment where vulnerability is dangerous; she called this emotional numbness. Such switching off is a defense, not heartlessness. From her point of view, you could say that indifference sometimes appears when there are too many feelings or they are too painful. The love ethic doesn't demand that you immediately feel the “right” thing; it offers patient attention — feelings come back when it becomes safe enough. The fact that you notice your indifference and are worried about it already speaks of living care.
indifference.practice: Ask yourself: if some feeling were hiding under the indifference, what might it be? Don't force an answer — just ask the question.

escape.text: The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — and go somewhere no one knows you says that your present life has become too cramped. It is a legitimate feeling. bell hooks herself changed her life more than once: she moved, left prestigious positions, and in the end returned to her native Kentucky. But she described change as a choice grounded in values, not as running away from pain. From her point of view, you could say that the dream of escape hints at what you are missing — freedom, rest, meaning, community. It is worth listening to without rushing to tear anything down. Sometimes a small change is enough to make it easier to breathe; sometimes the dream gradually turns into a well-considered plan.
escape.practice: Finish the sentence: “If I left, I would finally be able to…”. Think about what small piece of that is possible already now.

forbidden_attraction.text: An attraction to someone you “mustn't” be attracted to — someone unavailable, “the wrong” person — can be confusing and frightening. The feeling itself doesn't make you bad: desire doesn't ask permission. In All About Love and Communion bell hooks distinguished attraction, infatuation and love. Infatuation, she wrote, often rests on fantasy and projection — we see in the other what we lack, and that is not yet knowing the person. Love, by contrast, requires knowledge, time and mutuality. From her point of view, you could say that such an attraction can tell you a lot about yourself — about a longing for aliveness, attention, freedom. You can explore it calmly, without rushing to conclusions about yourself.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down which qualities or feelings draw you in when you are near this person. Ask yourself which of these you are missing in your life in general.

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment can turn a simple meeting into an ordeal. It is a very common feeling, and it doesn't mean something is wrong with you. bell hooks wrote a lot about “voice” — the right to speak and be heard. In Talking Back she recalled how as a child she was scolded for “talking back” to adults, and how speaking in her own voice became an act of courage for her. In Teaching to Transgress she strove for a classroom where every voice is valued and no one fears ridicule. From her point of view, you could say that fear of judgment grows where we were measured and shamed, and weakens in spaces of respect. Such spaces can be sought out — starting small.
social_anxiety.practice: Think of someone around whom you feel at ease. What exactly do they do that makes you feel safe? Write it down — it will show you where to look for support.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is draining: it's hard to plan and hard to relax when you don't know what will happen. That is a normal reaction. Following Paulo Freire, bell hooks spoke of education as “the practice of freedom,” and freedom, as she understood it, always involves risk: to learn is to enter a place where there are no ready-made answers in advance. She didn't promise guarantees and didn't believe life can be fully controlled. From her point of view, you could say that uncertainty is not only a threat but also a space of possibility, where not everything has been decided for you yet. This doesn't cancel the anxiety, but it gives it neighbors — curiosity and hope.
uncertainty.practice: Make two columns: “what I don't know” and “what I know for sure.” In the second column, find at least one thing to lean on.

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, a reply, news — stretches time and keeps you suspended. It is hard, and impatience is understandable. bell hooks wrote about love as a patient practice: commitment, one of its ingredients, shows itself over time, not in a single moment. From her point of view, you could say that while waiting we often live entirely in the future, and the present is left without attention. The practice of mindfulness she held dear, which came to her from Thich Nhat Hanh, brings you back to what is happening now: to your breath, to the person beside you, to the task in your hands. Waiting doesn't have to be empty time — it can become a time of caring for yourself while the answer is still on its way.
waiting.practice: For the time you're waiting, choose one simple thing that feels like care — a walk, a call, an unhurried meal — and do it today.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do can come back again and again. It shows that you care how your life turns out, and it speaks of values that may now be clearer to you. bell hooks wrote that love requires honesty, above all with yourself: looking at the past without embellishment and without cruelty. For her, responsibility is not endless guilt but the ability to learn from experience and act differently. From her point of view, you could say that regret is knowledge you didn't have back then. You can't carry it into the past, but you can bring it into the present — into how you live, love and choose today. Back then you were who you were able to be.
regret.practice: Write: “Back then I didn't know…, and now I know…”. Think about where this knowledge could be useful as soon as this week.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is love looking for somewhere to go. It can be quiet or sharp, but it always speaks of a bond that matters to you. bell hooks wrote that love doesn't vanish when a person is far away: care, memory and gratitude go on living in us and in what we do. She also insisted that one person shouldn't be your only source of warmth: we need circles of community, friends, people with whom to share life. From her point of view, you could say that longing is a sign of your ability to attach, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. You can hold it gently while staying open to other connections too.
longing.practice: Write this person a letter — whether to send it you can decide later. Tell them what you remember and what you're grateful for.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from news of war, cruelty, injustice — shows that your heart hasn't closed. It is a heavy feeling, and carrying it alone is almost impossible. bell hooks believed that love concerns more than private life: a love ethic, in her view, should also guide how people treat one another beyond the family. But she also knew that despair is depleting, and she found support in community and spiritual practice. From her point of view, you could say that you don't need to absorb all the pain of the world to prove your sensitivity. You can choose how much news to take in, look after yourself, and do something small and concrete where you are.
world_pain.practice: Today, limit the news to one window of time. Think of one small act of kindness in your surroundings — and do it.

rejection.text: Rejection — when you weren't chosen, weren't accepted, weren't wanted — hurts, and this pain is very ancient: people have always needed to belong. bell hooks wrote that many of us have linked love with conditions since childhood: we are loved if we are “good,” convenient, successful. That's why a refusal so easily sounds like a verdict on the whole person. But for hooks, love begins with self-love — with self-esteem that doesn't depend on other people's approval. From her point of view, you could say that rejection speaks of the other's decision, limitations or tastes, of a mismatch, not of your worth. It hurts because you opened up — and that openness remains your strength.
rejection.practice: Write down what exactly was rejected — a specific proposal, application, step. Then add: “But not me as a whole.”

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can run very deep: it makes you cling, check, and panic at any sign of coolness. It is often rooted in early experience, when care was unreliable. bell hooks wrote that many people grew up in families where love was mixed with unpredictability, and later carry that expectation into adult relationships. None of this is your fault. For hooks, an important part of healing is learning to give yourself the reliability that was once missing, and building relationships on trust and honest communication. From her point of view, you could say that your fear is the trace of an old wound, not a prophecy. Today you have the chance to care for yourself and to seek out people who stay.
abandonment.practice: Recall a person or situation where you weren't left, even though you feared you would be. Write it down — as a reminder that this happens too.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is a feeling with nowhere to return to, and that is why it hurts so sharply. Your love is no less real because of it. bell hooks distinguished infatuation from love: infatuation often rests on a fantasy about the other, while love requires mutuality — knowledge, trust and commitment on both sides. From her point of view, you could say that unrequited love is a genuine capacity to love that hasn't yet found a mutual space, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. But hooks also reminded us that love is care for growth, including your own: sometimes loving yourself means ceasing to wait for an answer where there is none, and directing your warmth to where it can be received.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love has taught you about what you value in people. These qualities are a compass, not a loss.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: as if your dignity had been taken from you in front of others. If someone treated you this way, the responsibility lies with the one who humiliated you. bell hooks wrote that humiliation and shaming often serve as tools of power — in families, schools, workplaces — and have nothing to do with love or care. Her love ethic is based on recognition: seeing in everyone a person worthy of respect. From her point of view, you could say that your dignity is not defined by how you were treated; it can be wounded but not taken away. Healing begins when you can tell what you went through to people who respect you.
humiliation.practice: Write yourself a sentence you would like to hear from someone who is on your side. Read it out loud.

quote.text: Abuse and neglect negate love. Care and affirmation, the opposite of abuse and humiliation, are the foundation of love.
quote.author: bell hooks

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with one's body is familiar to a great many people, and it rarely arises on its own. In Feminism Is for Everybody bell hooks devoted a chapter to beauty: she showed how culture and advertising impose narrow standards of appearance, especially on women, and how people begin to look at themselves through someone else's eyes. In Black Looks she wrote about how media images teach people to be ashamed of their looks, their skin color, their features. From her point of view, you could say that your shame about your body is largely learned, not deserved. Self-love, for hooks, includes caring for your body as a home rather than as a project to be fixed. You can treat it gently already now.
body_shame.practice: Name one thing your body did for you today — carried you, warmed you, let you see something. Thank it for that.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, your usual sense of yourself collapses: plans, strength, independence. It is hard, and fear, anger or sadness are entirely fitting here. bell hooks wrote little about illness directly, but her idea of love as care matters especially here. She criticized a culture that ranks independence and productivity so highly that asking for help seems like weakness. From her point of view, you could say that interdependence is not a failure but part of human life, since each of us at some point needs the care of others. Illness does not lessen your worth. Letting others care for you is also a way of taking part in love, and gentleness toward yourself now is not a whim but a necessity.
illness.practice: Name one specific thing you could use help with right now, and one person you could ask.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a healthy and well-earned feeling, and you can enjoy it. bell hooks, who grew up in a working-class family in the American South and became a professor and the author of more than thirty books, knew well the cost of such a path. She called self-esteem the foundation of self-love: acknowledging your work, your growth, your strengths. At the same time, for hooks pride is fullest when it is seen and shared: one person's success almost always rests on the support of many — teachers, family, community. From her point of view, you could say that being proud of yourself is not immodest; it is a form of recognition, and recognition is one of the ingredients of love. Name what you have done, and those who helped you along the way.
pride.practice: Write down what you are proud of, and the name of someone you'd like to tell about it or thank.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a quiet, pensive feeling in which sorrow is joined with tenderness. You don't have to do anything with it. bell hooks loved poetry and wrote poems herself; writing was for her a space where deep feelings could be lived through and reflected on. In Belonging she describes with tenderness and sadness her native hills, loved ones who are gone, a vanished way of life — and this sadness doesn't break her but connects her with what she loved. From her point of view, you could say that melancholy is a way of remembering and cherishing. It doesn't need fixing — only space and, perhaps, words.
melancholy.practice: Write a few lines about what brings on this gentle sadness — not a report, but almost a poem.
